title: Visual Attention in Children
abstract: Speech perception is inherently multimodal during face-to-face conversations: we both hear and see the talker. Infants are able to integrate audiovisual speech cues from early in life. Recent evidence suggests that they also flexibly shift their visual attention to a talker’s lips in conditions when speech is unfamiliar. The present study aimed to extend this work. Specifically, we tested the hypothesis that children will flexibly alter their visual attention to talkers when speech input is degraded. The rationale for this study is that naturalistic environments of children often contain background noise that disrupts the fidelity of the acoustic parts of speech. Participants were typically-developing children between 3 and 5 years of age. To quantify visual attention, we utilized an eye-tracking paradigm which assesses the location and duration of a participant’s eye gaze to the talker and images of known words as speech was unfolding, in quiet and in the presence of two-talker background speech presented at 10 dB signal-to-noise ratio. Consistent with our hypothesis, results showed that children visually fixated the talker to a greater extent in the background speech condition than in the quiet condition. The presentation will include discussion about how children’s speech recognition accuracy with or without visual speech cues as well as preliminary data from children with hearing loss. The data informs us about how young children flexibly alter their visual attention to talkers in less than ideal listening environments.
